about.en:
The International Olympiad in Informatics (IOI) is the most prestigious algorithmic programming competition for secondary-school students. IOI 2027 takes place in Potsdam, Germany, from 12 to 19 September 2027, hosted by the Hasso Plattner Institute; it is the first time Germany has hosted the olympiad in 35 years. Contestants solve hard algorithmic tasks in C++ over two five-hour competition days, and around half receive gold, silver or bronze medals.

You cannot register for the IOI as an individual. Each participating country runs its own national olympiad in informatics (often several online and on-site rounds plus a training camp) and selects a team of up to four students. Selection for the September 2027 team happens during the 2026/27 school year, so now is the time to find your national organiser (listed on ioinformatics.org under countries) and enter its first round. Many countries also pick teams for regional olympiads such as EGOI (girls), BOI, CEOI or APIO from the same rounds.

Why it matters: an IOI medal is one of the strongest signals a pre-university student can show to computer-science departments (MIT, ETH, Oxford, Cambridge and others) and to tech employers, and the training itself (dynamic programming, graphs, data structures) is excellent preparation for university CS. Host countries cover board and lodging for official delegations during the event.

Two 5-hour contest days of algorithmic problems; medals for about half of contestants

about.en:
The International Olympiad in Artificial Intelligence (IOAI) is an international science olympiad for high-school students, launched in 2024 (Bulgaria) and since held in China (2025) and Kazakhstan (2026). The 4th IOAI will be held in Singapore from 4 to 10 July 2027. Contestants work on scientific and practical AI problems, typically training and evaluating models in Python on a shared computing platform, plus team challenges, alongside a cultural programme with students from dozens of countries.

Countries take part through a National Olympiad in AI (NOAI), which selects the students who represent them; regional olympiads in AI also sit under the IOAI umbrella. Countries with little previous olympiad experience can join through the IOAI GAITE initiative. If your country has no national AI olympiad yet, ask your ministry, national STEM olympiad body or computer-science teachers' association to contact IOAI; individual students cannot enter on their own.

The IOAI is a rare chance for secondary students to show serious machine-learning skill at an international level, and its syllabus (classical ML, neural networks, computer vision, NLP) is a strong free study plan even if you do not make the team.

about.en:
The International Linguistics Olympiad (IOL) is one of the international science olympiads for secondary-school students. Problems give you data in a language you have almost certainly never seen (for example numbers, verb forms or a writing system) and ask you to deduce how it works. Every problem is self-contained, so no knowledge of linguistics or foreign languages is needed: what counts is logic, pattern-spotting and careful reasoning.

The 24th IOL will be held in Bangkok, Thailand, from 21 to 28 July 2027. It has an individual contest (five problems, six hours) and a team contest. Each participating country sends one or two teams of four students, usually chosen from the top scorers of its national linguistics olympiad (for example UKLO in the UK, NACLO in the USA and Canada, OzCLO in Australia, plus national olympiads across Europe and Asia). The IOL website lists the organiser in each country and how its team is chosen.

The IOL is a great fit for students who love languages, puzzles, maths or computer science, and a medal is a distinctive achievement for applications in linguistics, languages, computer science or philosophy. Past problems are freely available to practise.

about.en:
The European Girls' Mathematical Olympiad (EGMO) is a premier international mathematics competition for female secondary-school students. Founded by the United Kingdom in 2012, it now includes more than sixty countries, and many non-European countries take part as guests. Like the IMO, EGMO runs over two days with three olympiad problems each day (4.5 hours per paper); about half of contestants win medals.

EGMO 2027 takes place in Šibenik, Croatia, from 11 to 17 April 2027. Participation is by invitation through national mathematics olympiad organisers: each country nominates up to four girls, usually based on national olympiad results and team-selection tests held in winter. If you are a girl who enjoys competition maths, ask your national olympiad committee or maths teacher how the EGMO team is chosen and make sure you enter the national olympiad rounds this school year.

EGMO is a stepping stone to IMO teams and a strong credential for mathematics, computer science and engineering applications. It also builds a lasting international network of young women in mathematics.

about.en:
The International Chemistry Olympiad (IChO) is the most demanding chemistry competition for secondary-school students, held every July since 1968. The 59th IChO will be hosted by Chinese Taipei (Taiwan) from 19 to 28 July 2027. Students sit a five-hour practical laboratory exam and a five-hour theoretical exam covering organic, inorganic, physical and analytical chemistry at early-university level; roughly the top 60% receive medals.

Each participating country sends a team of up to four students plus mentors. There is no individual entry: students qualify through their national chemistry olympiad, which in most countries has a school round in autumn or winter, a national final and a training camp. The host publishes preparatory problems months in advance, which form an excellent free syllabus.

IChO medallists are sought after by top chemistry, medicine and natural-science programmes worldwide, and the training (lab technique, spectroscopy, kinetics, synthesis) puts students well ahead of their peers.

about.en:
The International Biology Olympiad (IBO) is the world's largest biology competition for secondary-school students. The 38th IBO will take place in Warsaw, Poland, from 18 to 25 July 2027. Students sit practical exams (usually three or four lab sessions of about 90 minutes in areas such as molecular biology, physiology, ecology and evolution) and theoretical exams of around 100 tasks applying biology to unfamiliar research data, alongside excursions and a cultural programme.

You cannot register with the IBO directly. You must win your National Biology Olympiad (NBO) and be selected for your country's team; each member country or region sends up to four students. What matters is the location of your school, not your nationality, and some countries exclude home-schooled or international-school students, so check with your national coordinator early.

An IBO medal is a strong credential for medicine, biology and life-science applications, and the national olympiad training itself is excellent preparation for university-level biology.

about.en:
Regeneron ISEF, run by the Society for Science, is the largest international science fair for high-school students. Each May, around 1,600–1,800 finalists from nearly every US state and more than 60 countries, regions and territories present original research projects in 22 categories, from biochemistry and robotics to behavioural science and environmental engineering. The 2027 fair will be held in Los Angeles, California, in May 2027 (exact dates to be published by the Society).

You cannot apply to ISEF directly. Students earn a place by winning at one of roughly 365 Society-affiliated science fairs worldwide: local, regional, state or national fairs that each nominate a set number of finalists. Many countries have a national ISEF-affiliated fair (for example national youth science competitions or ministry-run fairs), and the Society's 'Find a Fair' tool lists every affiliated fair and its contact. Projects must follow ISEF rules (research plan, adult sponsor, forms and, for human or animal subjects, prior review), so plan the paperwork before you start experiments.

Why it is worth it: finalists compete for top awards of up to USD 75,000 and hundreds of special awards and scholarships, meet scientists and Nobel laureates, and gain a credential valued by universities worldwide. Even if you do not reach ISEF, affiliated fairs give you judging feedback and a research portfolio.

about.en:
The Earth Prize is an annual global competition, based in Geneva, that challenges students aged 13 to 19 to design solutions to environmental sustainability problems. It describes itself as the world's largest environmental competition for young people, with teams from more than 160 countries and territories in its first editions. Students register free, learn through the organisers' educational resources, and submit a project idea (a product, service, policy or campaign) addressing a real environmental issue.

about.en:
The Orwell Youth Prize, run by the Orwell Foundation (the charity behind the Orwell Prizes for political writing), invites young people to write about their world in any form: essay, short story, poem, article, speech or script. The 2027 theme is 'Acts of Courage'. Word limits are 1,000 words for Years 7–11 and 1,500 words for Years 12–13, with categories for Years 7–9, 10–11 and 12–13.

A distinctive feature is free individual feedback: entries submitted by the feedback deadline of 3 March 2027 receive written comments from the Orwell team, and you can then revise before the final deadline of 28 April 2027. Winners and runners-up are celebrated at an awards event and published by the Foundation, and the programme includes workshops and a summer residential for selected writers.

Eligibility focuses on secondary students at school or college in the UK; the Foundation also mentions students following a British curriculum, so students at British international schools abroad should check the terms before entering.

eligibility.en: Secondary students in Years 7–13 (or equivalent) at school or college in the UK; British-curriculum students abroad should confirm eligibility in the terms and conditions. Entrants aged 12 or under need parent/guardian consent.

about.en:
The FIRST Robotics Competition (FRC) is the flagship high-school programme of FIRST, the non-profit founded by inventor Dean Kamen. Starting from a Kit of Parts, teams of students aged 14–18, guided by adult mentors, design, program and build a large robot to play a new game in three-team alliances. The 2027 game, BIOCORE presented by Haas, is part of the FIRST CANOPY season and will be released on 9 January 2027; teams then have a few weeks to build before district and regional events from late February to April.

Top teams advance to the FIRST Championship in Houston, Texas, from 28 April to 1 May 2027, the world's largest K-12 robotics event (in 2026: 50,000 attendees from 59 countries). Beyond the robot, teams run like small companies: they raise funds, do outreach, build a brand and compete for awards such as the FIRST Impact Award. In the 2024-25 season about 93,000 students from 35 countries took part.

FRC is ideal for students who want hands-on engineering, programming (Java, C++, Python), CAD and business experience. Participants get access to FIRST scholarships worth millions of dollars from partner universities and companies. If there is no team at your school, you can join a community team nearby or start one.

about.en:
FIRST Tech Challenge (FTC) is FIRST's robotics programme for students aged 12–18 (grades 7–12). Teams of up to about 15 students design, build and program robots from reusable kits to compete in alliance-based matches, and document their engineering process in a portfolio that is judged for awards. The 2026–27 game is BIOBUZZ presented by RTX, part of the FIRST CANOPY season, released in September 2026.

Teams play in league meets and qualifying tournaments from autumn to spring; top teams advance to regional or national championships and then the FIRST Championship in Houston on 28 April – 1 May 2027. FTC runs in many countries through FIRST Program Delivery Partners, and international teams regularly qualify for Houston.

FTC is cheaper and more accessible than the larger FIRST Robotics Competition while still teaching real engineering: CAD, Java or block programming, sensors and autonomous code. Students also gain access to FIRST scholarships and the FIRST Leadership Award.

FIRST LEGO League introduces younger students to engineering and coding. Teams use LEGO Education SPIKE technology: younger children (Explore, ages 6–10) build a model, while Challenge teams (ages 9–14 in most countries) program a robot to complete missions autonomously in 2½-minute matches, and also research a real-world problem and present an innovation project judged on core values.

The 2026–27 season is BIOGLOW Founders Edition, and FIRST has announced it will be the final season of FIRST LEGO League before its K-8 programmes change from 2027. Teams compete at regional and national tournaments, and top teams can be invited to international events and the FIRST Championship in Houston (28 April – 1 May 2027).

If your younger sibling or school wants a first robotics competition, this last season is a good moment to join: it runs in dozens of countries through national FIRST partners.

about.en:
The World Robot Olympiad (WRO) is a global robotics competition, running since 2004, that involved more than 100,000 students and 32,000 teams in 2025 across more than 100 countries. Teams of two or three students with a coach compete in four categories: RoboMission (programming a robot to solve a mission on a table, in Elementary, Junior and Senior age groups), RoboSports (robot vs. robot games), Future Innovators (designing a robotics solution on the season theme) and Future Engineers (autonomous self-driving cars, up to age 22).

Each season has a new theme and challenges published in January; the 2026 theme was 'Robots Meet Culture'. Teams first compete in their national WRO competition, run by the national organiser, who adapts the rules for that country. The best teams qualify for the WRO International Final, hosted in a different country each year (2025 Singapore; 2026 San Juan, Puerto Rico, 8–10 December 2026), and for regional Open Championships.

WRO is a great fit for students who like LEGO, Arduino or similar platforms, and the Future Engineers category is a serious challenge in autonomous driving. Check your national organiser now so your team is ready when the 2027 challenges are released.

about.en:
The GENIUS Olympiad is an international project-based competition for secondary-school students, founded around environmental and sustainability themes. Students submit a project in one of nine categories: AI, Art, Coding, Entrepreneurship, Music, Robotics, Science, Short Film and Speech. Selected finalists present at the finals, held from 7 to 12 June 2027 at St. John Fisher University in Rochester, New York, alongside students from many countries.

The application system opens in December 2026 and project applications are due on 1 March 2027 (09:00 US Eastern Time); affiliated fairs in the US and EU have a later deadline. Projects are reviewed by judges, and accepted finalists receive an invitation to the finals, where awards and medals are presented in each category.

GENIUS is one of the few international olympiads that welcomes both STEM and creative projects, so it suits students with a research, engineering, art or film portfolio who want international recognition. Note that finalists pay participation fees and travel.

about.en:
Technovation Challenge is a global technology-entrepreneurship programme run by Technovation, a US non-profit historically known for Technovation Girls. Builders aged 8 to 18 form teams in their own communities, identify a problem worth solving, and build a working tech or AI solution (a mobile app or AI project), along with a pitch video and business or impact plan. Teams are supported by volunteer mentors and Chapter Leaders, who run the programme in about 160 countries; in 2026, 12,000 learners from 130 countries took part.

The season runs from October to May, with teams competing in Beginner, Junior and Senior divisions by age. Registration for the 2027 season opened in October 2026. Submissions are judged online, and finalists from each division earn a place at the Technovation World Summit to pitch to industry leaders and judges.

It is an excellent first entrepreneurship and coding project: the free curriculum teaches app development (for example MIT App Inventor), AI basics and pitching, and the work produces a portfolio piece for applications. Older alumni can continue to the AI Ventures Accelerator (ages 19–24).

about.en:
The USA Computing Olympiad (USACO) runs free online programming contests and training for high-school students; it selects the US team for the International Olympiad in Informatics, but its online contests are taken by many thousands of students worldwide as olympiad practice. Contestants solve three algorithmic problems in a few hours in C++, Java or Python, and move up through Bronze, Silver, Gold and Platinum divisions as their scores improve.

The 2025–26 season was restructured: three online contests in January and February 2026, followed by an invitational proctored US Open for top US students. The 2026–27 schedule has not yet been posted (as of 30 October 2026); expect the online contests again in winter. Any student can create a free account and compete; only US students are eligible for the US team and camp, but international students receive scores and division promotions.

USACO's free training pages and its large archive of past problems with solutions make it one of the best self-study paths into competitive programming, whatever your country's olympiad.

about.en:
CS50x is the OpenCourseWare version of CS50, Harvard University's introductory computer-science course taught by David J. Malan. Anyone can take it free: you work through eleven weeks of lectures, sections and shorts covering Scratch, C, arrays, algorithms, memory, data structures, Python, SQL, artificial intelligence and web development (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Flask), then build a final project of your own choice.

Problem sets are submitted online and graded automatically, and you can ask questions in CS50's large online communities and through CS50.ai, a course-specific AI tutor. If you score at least 70% on every problem set and the final project, you receive a free CS50 Certificate; a verified certificate is available for a fee via edX (cs50.edx.org). The 2026 edition is open now; according to the course FAQ, work must be finished by end of day 30 June 2027, and work submitted since 2025 carries forward if the course is extended.

CS50x is widely considered the best first course in programming for motivated beginners, and the final project is a strong portfolio item for university applications in CS or engineering. Lectures are also dubbed into Portuguese and Spanish.

about.en:
OpenWHO is the World Health Organization's interactive, web-based knowledge-transfer platform. It offers free online courses on health emergencies and outbreaks, infectious diseases, vaccination, mental health, clinical management, and public-health skills, created by WHO experts. Courses are available in many languages, including Arabic and other UN languages, and many are designed for frontline responders as well as the general public.

Anyone can register free and enrol at any time. Courses are short and self-paced; learners who complete the assessments usually receive a free Record of Achievement or Confirmation of Participation.

For students interested in medicine, global health or WHO-themed MUN committees, OpenWHO provides authoritative, certified learning straight from the source.

Free certificates (Record of Achievement)
Dozens of languages

about.en:
The Open Learning Campus (OLC) is the World Bank Group's learning platform, offering e-learning courses, webinars and talks on development topics: poverty and inequality, public finance, education and health systems, climate change and disaster risk, energy, infrastructure, governance, gender, and data and evaluation. Many self-paced e-courses are free to the public and award a certificate on completion of the assessments.

You need to create a free account to enrol (the site opens with a sign-in page). Content is aimed at policymakers and development professionals, so it is best for university students or ambitious secondary students interested in economics, public policy or international relations.

OLC courses provide authoritative background for economics essays, MUN committees on development, and applications to economics or policy degrees.

Free certificates on many self-paced courses
Development economics, climate and policy topics

about.en:
Elements of AI is a free online course created by the University of Helsinki and MinnaLearn to teach the basics of artificial intelligence to anyone. Its six chapters explain what AI is, problem solving with search, real-world AI and probability, machine learning, neural networks, and the implications of AI for society, using clear explanations and exercises rather than programming. A follow-up course, Building AI, introduces simple Python implementations.

The course is self-paced, available in many languages (with national versions across Europe and a global English version), and has been completed by more than 2 million people. Completing the exercises earns a free certificate from the University of Helsinki (and, for students at some institutions, ECTS credits).

It is an ideal first step for students curious about AI, and a credible certificate to show interest in AI ethics or technology on a university application.

en: Free certificate from the University of Helsinki
No maths or coding required
Many language versions

eligibility.en: Anyone, worldwide. No prerequisites.

Download your certificate; continue with Building AI if you want to code.

about.en:
Microsoft Learn is Microsoft's free learning platform. It offers thousands of short, interactive modules grouped into learning paths, covering AI fundamentals, Azure cloud, data analysis, Power BI, Python and C#, GitHub, cybersecurity and Microsoft 365 tools, often with free sandbox environments for practice. Learners earn badges and trophies on their Microsoft Learn profile.

Learning is free with a Microsoft account. Learning paths map to Microsoft role-based certifications (for example AI-900 Azure AI Fundamentals); exams are paid, but students sometimes access discounted vouchers through school or Microsoft programmes.

It is a practical way to build job-ready tech skills and a verifiable learning record.

en: Thousands of free interactive modules
Free practice sandboxes
Paths aligned to Microsoft certifications

eligibility.en: Anyone with a free Microsoft account.

Optionally book a certification exam.

about.en:
freeCodeCamp is a non-profit that has helped millions of people learn to code for free. Its interactive curriculum runs in the browser and leads to free certifications, including Responsive Web Design, JavaScript, Front End Libraries, Back End and APIs, Relational Databases, Python, Data Analysis with Python, Machine Learning with Python and more. Each certification requires completing required projects that you build yourself.

There are no fees and no deadlines; you sign in with a free account and progress is saved. freeCodeCamp also hosts thousands of free articles and full-length video courses (including CS50 courses on its YouTube channel).

Completed certifications are verifiable online and the projects form a portfolio, useful for internships and for showing initiative on university applications.

Project-based curriculum
No deadlines

about.en:
The Science of Well-Being is Yale University's most popular online course, taught by psychology professor Laurie Santos. Over six modules it explains common misconceptions about happiness (money, grades, possessions), the biases that make our minds mislead us, and the research-based strategies that actually improve well-being, such as gratitude, social connection, exercise, sleep and savouring. Learners complete a 'rewirement' challenge, practising one habit for several weeks.

More than 5 million people have enrolled. The course takes about 10 hours, is self-paced, and has subtitles in 24 languages; Yale also offers a teen version for younger students.

It is a great choice for students handling exam stress or university applications, and an easy, respected certificate for any CV.

Evidence-based habits for happiness and stress

about.en:
Learning How to Learn: Powerful mental tools to help you master tough subjects gives practical, neuroscience-based techniques used by experts in art, music, literature, maths, science and sport. It covers focused and diffuse modes of thinking, chunking, spaced repetition, the Pomodoro technique for procrastination, memory techniques, and how to prepare for tests. The instructors are Dr Barbara Oakley and Professor Terrence Sejnowski (Salk Institute / UC San Diego).

More than 4 million learners have enrolled; the course is beginner level, self-paced, and available with subtitles in 25 languages, with fully translated Portuguese and Spanish versions.

It is one of the best investments a student can make before exams, olympiad training or a demanding university course.

about.en:
The Machine Learning Specialization, created by Stanford Online and DeepLearning.AI and taught by AI pioneer Andrew Ng, is the updated version of his famous Stanford machine-learning course. Its three courses cover supervised learning (linear and logistic regression), advanced learning algorithms (neural networks with TensorFlow, decision trees, practical advice for building ML systems) and unsupervised learning, recommender systems and reinforcement learning. Each week includes optional and graded Jupyter notebook labs in Python.

The programme is beginner-friendly (high-school algebra and basic Python suffice), takes about two months at 10 hours a week, and has subtitles in 30 languages; more than 850,000 learners have enrolled.

It is a recognised first credential in machine learning and excellent preparation for the International Olympiad in AI or AI research projects.

about.en:
Python for Everybody is a five-course specialization from the University of Michigan taught by Professor Charles 'Dr Chuck' Severance. It starts with the basics of programming (variables, loops, functions), then moves to Python data structures, accessing web data (HTML, XML, JSON, APIs), using databases with SQL, and a capstone project retrieving, processing and visualising data.

It assumes no prior programming experience, takes about two months at 10 hours a week, and has subtitles in 27 languages. More than 2 million learners have enrolled.

It is one of the most beginner-friendly routes into programming and data analysis, and suits students who want practical skills for science projects, economics or computing.

about.en:
Financial Markets, taught by Yale professor and Nobel laureate Robert Shiller, gives an overview of the ideas, methods and institutions that let society manage risk and foster enterprise. Topics include risk management and insurance, the Capital Asset Pricing Model, efficient markets and behavioural finance, stocks, bonds and real estate, central banks and monetary policy, investment banking, and the ethics of finance.

The course is beginner level, self-paced, and has more than 2.4 million learners with subtitles in 22 languages.

It is excellent preparation for economics or finance degrees, essay competitions in economics, and investment challenges.

Beginner level; 2.4M+ learners

about.en:
AI For Everyone, created by DeepLearning.AI and taught by Andrew Ng, explains artificial intelligence for non-engineers: common AI terminology (machine learning, deep learning, data science), what AI can realistically do, how to choose and run AI projects, how AI fits into companies, and the ethical and societal questions it raises.

The course takes about 7 hours over four modules, is beginner level and has subtitles in 27 languages; more than 2.6 million learners have enrolled.

It gives students the vocabulary to discuss AI in essays, debates and MUN committees and is a gentle introduction before technical courses like CS50 AI or the Machine Learning Specialization.

about.en:
Practical Deep Learning for Coders, by Jeremy Howard and fast.ai, teaches deep learning 'top-down': you build and deploy working models first and learn the theory as you go. Its nine lessons (about 90 minutes each) cover computer vision, natural-language processing, tabular data, collaborative filtering, and the foundations of neural networks, using PyTorch, fastai and Hugging Face libraries. A second part (30+ hours) goes deeper into the foundations of Stable Diffusion-style models.

It is free, needs no special hardware (it shows how to use free cloud notebooks), and does not require university maths, only some coding experience (ideally Python). It is based on the free online book 'Deep Learning for Coders with fastai and PyTorch'.

Many AI practitioners started here; it is ideal for students preparing AI projects, Kaggle competitions or the IOAI.

Courses are self-paced, use Python and free notebooks, and several (such as the Agents and Deep RL courses) award free certificates for completing assignments.

They are ideal for students who already code in Python and want to build real projects with modern open-source AI models.

The UN Women Training Centre eLearning Campus is a global online platform for training on gender equality and women's empowerment, open to everybody interested in using training as a means of transformation. Courses range from the self-paced introductory series 'I Know Gender' (gender concepts, international frameworks, and gender in areas such as work, health, education and peace) to moderated, specialised courses for professionals.

The campus is available in English, Spanish, French and Arabic. You register for a free account; many self-paced courses are free and issue a certificate on completion, while some moderated courses have fees or are for UN staff.

These courses help students working on human-rights projects, MUN committees (UN Women, CSW, UNHRC) and youth leadership programmes.

about.en:
Saylor Academy is a non-profit that has offered free, self-paced online courses since 2008, with more than 3 million students enrolled. Its catalogue of 160+ courses covers business administration, computer science, mathematics (from pre-calculus to calculus and statistics), science, social sciences, arts and humanities, and English as a second language, plus specialization programmes. Courses use open educational resources and end with a final exam; passing earns a free certificate.

Some Saylor courses are recommended for college credit by external evaluators, and Saylor offers degree programmes for those who want to go further.

For students, it is a structured, free way to study a subject in depth (for example to prepare for AP, A-level or first-year university courses) with proof of completion.

about.en:
Machine Learning Crash Course (MLCC) is Google's free introduction to machine learning, relied on by millions of people since 2018 and refreshed with a stronger focus on interactive learning. Self-contained modules cover ML models (linear and logistic regression, classification), working with data (numerical and categorical data, datasets, generalisation and overfitting), advanced models (neural networks, embeddings, large language models) and real-world ML (production systems, AutoML, fairness).

Each module combines short videos, interactive visualisations and programming exercises in Colab notebooks. It is free and needs only a Google account for the exercises; there is no formal certificate.

It is a fast, credible way to understand how ML works before IOAI preparation, a research project or the Stanford/DeepLearning.AI specialization.

Its free self-paced catalogue includes Python Essentials 1 (no prior experience necessary), Introduction to Cybersecurity, Networking Basics, Introduction to IoT, Introduction to Data Science and more.

Python Essentials 1, developed with the OpenEDG Python Institute, teaches programming fundamentals and prepares learners for the entry-level PCEP certification exam (exam is separate and paid). Completers of NetAcad courses earn shareable Cisco digital badges.

NetAcad is a practical path to job-ready IT and cybersecurity skills, and many secondary schools and universities worldwide teach its courses in class.

It offers Arabic-language courses for individuals and business owners: job preparation, communication and productivity, digital marketing, programming and development, AI basics, cloud computing basics, online safety, design and sustainability. Introductory courses are hosted on Google's Skillshop catalogue, with more advanced cloud learning on Google Skills.

The site also links to Google Career Certificates (IT support, data analytics, UX design and more), which are professional programmes delivered through Coursera; these are paid but often available through scholarships and financial aid.

For Arabic-speaking students, it is one of the easiest ways to learn practical digital and AI skills in their own language.

Completing learning content earns shareable digital badges. No credit card is required.

Cloud skills are increasingly expected in computer-science and data careers; AWS Educate is a safe, free sandbox to start.

about.en:
The International Geography Olympiad (iGeo), held under the auspices of the International Geographical Union, is an annual competition for the best geography students aged 16 to 19. It has grown from five countries in 1996 to around 50 today. The 2027 iGeo takes place in Jelgava, Latvia, from 2 to 9 August 2027 (future hosts: Melbourne, Australia, in 2028 and Burgas, Bulgaria, in 2029).

The competition has three parts: a written response test (about 40% of marks), a fieldwork exercise in the host region in which students collect data and produce a map and analysis (about 40%), and a multimedia test (about 20%). It also includes a poster presentation and a cultural programme with students from every continent.

Students are chosen from the thousands who take part in their own National Geography Olympiads; each country sends a team of four. iGeo is a distinctive achievement for applications in geography, environmental science, urban planning or international relations, and the fieldwork element is a genuine research experience.

about.en:
The International Economics Olympiad (IEO) is an annual competition for high-school students in economics and finance, supported by Nobel laureate Eric Maskin. It brings together teams from around 74 countries, with more than 600,000 students taking part in national competitions each year. The olympiad includes individual rounds on economics and financial literacy and a team business case, all in English.

Each country is represented by one team of up to five contestants, selected by a long-term national partner (the 'Sending Organization'). Contestants must have been born less than 20 years before 30 June 2027 and be working toward a secondary-school diploma. The IEO 2027 annual regulations have been published; the host and exact dates are still to be announced, and the olympiad normally takes place on site in July or August. The host covers accommodation and full board for contestants and team leaders.

If your country is on the IEO participating-countries list, find the national competition there and enter this school year; if not, the IEO invites organisations to contact it to set up a national selection. It is a strong credential for economics, business and finance applications.

about.en:
The International Young Physicists' Tournament (IYPT), sometimes called the 'Physics World Cup', is a team competition for secondary-school students. Instead of a timed exam, teams spend months investigating 17 open-ended problems (real phenomena to model, measure and explain), then present and defend their research in 'Physics Fights' where teams take the roles of reporter, opponent and reviewer in front of a jury.

The 40th IYPT will be held in Auckland, New Zealand, from 5 to 12 July 2027. The 17 problems for 2027 were published on 15 July 2026 on iypt.org, so national teams are already working on them. Teams are registered by authorised IYPT member organisations; pre-registration closes on 15 December 2026.

Students usually reach the IYPT through a national young physicists' tournament or selection organised by their country's member organisation. It is excellent preparation for real research, scientific English and argumentation, and is highly regarded by physics and engineering departments.

about.en:
The International Mathematical Modeling Challenge (IM²C) is a team competition for secondary-school students that focuses on mathematical modelling: turning an open, real-world problem (for example scheduling, resource allocation or risk) into mathematics, solving it, testing assumptions and communicating the result in a written report. Unlike olympiads, there is no single right answer; judges reward sound reasoning, creativity and clear writing.

The 2027 IM²C starts on 1 February 2027. Teams (typically up to four students with a faculty advisor) work on the problem during a period of consecutive days within the contest window, at school and with any resources except outside help. The challenge runs through regional and national competitions in 54 countries and regions, whose best reports go forward to international judging; top teams are recognised at the IM²C summit.

It is ideal for students who like applied maths, data, economics or engineering, and the report is an impressive research-style writing sample.

The FIRST Global Challenge is an annual international robotics competition, often called the 'Olympics of robotics', in which one team of students aged roughly 14–18 represents each participating country. Teams from more than 190 countries receive the same robot kit and build robots to play a game themed around a global challenge (recent themes include energy, carbon capture, food security and ocean health), competing in cooperative alliances rather than country against country.

FIRST Global has announced that the 2027 Challenge will be held in Madrid, Spain; the 2026 edition took place on 7–10 October 2026 in the Republic of Korea. Dates, venue and the 2027 theme will be published on first.global.

Each country's team is recruited by a national team organiser (often a ministry, university or STEM non-profit). If you are interested, contact your country's current team via the National Teams pages or FIRST Global's contact form, since recruitment usually starts in the first half of the year.

about.en:
The Intermediate Mathematical Challenge (IMC) from the UK Mathematics Trust is a 60-minute, 25-question multiple-choice paper designed to encourage mathematical reasoning, precision of thought and fluency. Questions start accessible and become genuinely challenging, so it suits a wide range of students. It is taken by hundreds of thousands of students each year in UK schools and in overseas schools (for England, Wales and overseas: Year 11 and below).

In 2026–27 the challenge is sat on Wednesday 27 January 2027, on paper. Schools register with UKMT and buy entries: posted papers must be bought by 6 January 2027, downloadable papers by 27 January 2027, and answer sheets uploaded by 28 January 2027. Certificates are awarded, and the highest scorers are invited to the follow-on rounds (Grey and Pink Kangaroo, and the Cayley, Hamilton and Maclaurin Olympiads).

It is a respected, inexpensive way for British-curriculum and other international schools to give students an olympiad pathway, with free past papers and video solutions on the UKMT site.

about.en:
The Commonwealth Short Story Prize, run by the Commonwealth Foundation, is awarded for the best piece of unpublished short fiction (2,000–5,000 words) in English or translated into English. Stories are judged in five regions (Africa, Asia, Canada and Europe, the Caribbean, and the Pacific); regional winners are published by the literary magazine Granta and the overall winner receives a cash prize. Entries can be submitted in several languages besides English, which makes it unusually accessible.

For 2027, the Foundation has postponed the opening of the prize until January 2027 so it can comprehensively review its processes, entry rules and submission guidelines, including how to respond to AI-generated writing. Full rules and the closing date will be published when entries open.

It is free to enter and is one of the most respected routes to international publication for emerging writers aged 18 and over from Commonwealth countries.

about.en:
Advent of Code is an advent calendar of small programming puzzles for a variety of skill levels, created by Eric Wastl and running every December since 2015. Each day a new two-part puzzle unlocks; you solve it in any programming language and submit the answer computed from your personal input. Puzzles start gentle and grow harder, touching on parsing, simulation, graphs, dynamic programming and optimisation.

The 2026 event starts on 1 December 2026. It is free (supporters can optionally buy AoC++), needs only a login via an existing account (such as GitHub or Google), and puzzles remain available after December, so you can work through them at your own pace. Schools and clubs can create private leaderboards to compete with each other.

People use Advent of Code as interview preparation, company training, university coursework and speed-coding practice; for school students it is a fun daily habit that builds the problem-solving skills needed for USACO, national olympiads and the CCC.

Teams design, build and program fully autonomous robots in three leagues: Soccer (robots play two-versus-two football), Rescue (Line, Maze and Simulation: robots navigate a disaster scene and find 'victims'), and OnStage (creative robot performances). Teams also present their engineering process to judges.

RoboCup 2027, including the RoboCupJunior International Competition, will be held from 17 to 21 June 2027 at the Nuremberg Exhibition Center in Germany, hosted by RoboCup Germany (details on 2027.robocup.org). Teams qualify through their own region's events: talk to your Regional Representative about qualifying competitions, and see RoboCupJunior's 'Qualification and Competitions' page; there is still time to start a team this season.

It is an excellent path into robotics, embedded programming and AI, with super-regional events in Asia-Pacific, the Americas and Europe as well.

about.en:
The Stockholm Junior Water Prize (SJWP) is an international competition for students aged 15 to 20 who develop innovative research projects addressing major water challenges: water quality and treatment, scarcity, sanitation, microplastics, ecosystems or water-related technology. It has been held annually since 1997 and attracts tens of thousands of participants from around 40 countries.

Students first compete in their national SJWP competition (often run by a water association, science-fair body or ministry). National winners travel to Stockholm for the international final during World Water Week, where a jury of international water experts evaluates their projects and the prize is presented by the patron, H.R.H. Crown Princess Victoria of Sweden. Finalists also join a global alumni community, and the 2026 prize went to a Canadian student's robot that removes plastic from water while sparing marine life.

It is an outstanding goal for students doing environmental or engineering research, and national rounds often double as science-fair qualifiers.

about.en:
The World Scholar's Cup (WSC) is an international academic programme for students roughly 10 to 18, organised in junior and senior divisions. Teams of three study a yearly theme spanning science and technology, social studies, history, literature and a special area, then compete in four events: Team Debate, Collaborative Writing, the Scholar's Challenge (individual multiple-choice) and the Scholar's Bowl (team quiz). Schools can field unlimited teams.

The season starts with regional rounds in more than 100 cities worldwide (for 2026–27 these began in late October 2026, e.g. Al Ain, Kuwait, Haikou and Dalian). Qualifying teams advance to Global Rounds (for example a Tokyo-Yokohama Global Round on 11–15 December 2026) and then to the Tournament of Champions at Yale University; the 2026 Tournament of Champions took place on 12–18 November 2026. The calendar for the rest of the season is being posted over the coming weeks.

WSC is famous for being welcoming and fun (medals for many participants, a 'Scholar's Ball'), while building debate, writing and research skills. It is especially popular in Asia, the Middle East and Australia.

Major League Hacking (MLH) is the official student hackathon league. Its 2027 season calendar lists hundreds of in-person and some online hackathons run by student organisers at universities and high schools, mostly in North America and Europe but also in India and elsewhere. At a hackathon, you spend a weekend (24–48 hours) building a software or hardware project with a team, attend workshops, meet sponsor engineers and compete for prizes.

Examples on the current schedule include hackCBS in New Delhi (31 October – 1 November 2026), HackTheBurgh in Edinburgh, DurHack in Durham, UniHack in Timișoara and Junction in Espoo, Finland (13–15 November 2026), and HackPrinceton (13–15 November 2026). You can filter by region, diversity-focused events, high-school events and hardware labs.

Most MLH member events are free for students and provide food and swag; some offer travel reimbursement. It is the easiest way to find a reputable hackathon near you and to build a portfolio of projects.

The 2027 theme, 'Nature of Truth', asks students to explore environmental disinformation across natural and digital landscapes: how misinformation shapes what we believe about nature, and how creative work can tell the truth about it.

Students aged 11–18 enter in two divisions (Junior 11–14, Senior 15–18) and seven categories: Visual Art (Handcrafted), Visual Art (Digital), Poetry & Spoken Word, Creative Writing, Film, Performing Arts (Music & Dance), and Interactive & Multimedia. You can enter individually or as a club, class or group; each entry needs an adult sponsor. The deadline is 7 June 2027 at 11:59 pm EDT.

Winners receive cash awards of up to USD 1,000, and all participants receive a certificate; selected work may be exhibited or published. It is one of the best free international outlets for young artists and writers who care about the environment.

about.en:
The International Mathematical Tournament of Towns is a long-running olympiad-style competition in which cities, rather than countries, take part. It is run by local organising committees in more than 100 cities in over 25 countries. Each season has an autumn and a spring round, each with a basic O-level and a harder A-level paper of proof-based problems; results are scaled by city population.

Students in grades 8–11 take part (juniors grades 8–9, seniors 10–11; you may write a higher grade's paper). The autumn 2026 round took place on 4 October (O-level) and 18 October 2026 (A-level); the spring 2027 dates are to be announced on the official site. Participation is free for school students.

Tournament of Towns problems are elegant and highly regarded; top performers receive diplomas and invitations to a summer conference. If your city is not on the list, a teacher or university can apply to become a local committee.

en: Free; grades 8–11
O-level and A-level papers
100+ cities in 25+ countries

eligibility.en: School students in grades 8–11 in a participating city (via the local committee).

en: Check the list of participating cities on turgor.ru/en.
Contact your city's local committee to register for the spring 2027 round.
Practise with past Tournament of Towns problems.
Write the O-level and/or A-level paper on the announced dates.

costs.en: Free for students (local committees may accept voluntary contributions).

score_reason: Free and respected; spring dates TBA and city-dependent

about.en:
CS50's Introduction to Programming with Scratch is a free course from Harvard's CS50 team for absolute beginners, including younger students. Using Scratch, a visual block-based language from MIT, learners build animations, games and interactive stories while learning core ideas of programming: functions, conditionals, loops, variables and events.

Like other CS50 OpenCourseWare, it is free: watch the lectures, complete the problem sets and a final project, and receive a free CS50 certificate (a paid verified certificate is optional via edX).

It is an ideal first step before CS50x or CS50P, and a good recommendation for younger siblings or school coding clubs.

en: No experience needed; visual programming
Free CS50 certificate
Perfect bridge to CS50x

eligibility.en: Anyone; good for children and teenagers. Free edX account needed to submit work.

Complete each problem set and the final project.
Claim your free CS50 certificate.

IBM SkillsBuild offers 100% free learning in in-demand technology areas: artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, data analytics, cloud, IT support and professional skills. Courses are self-paced and range from short introductions to longer learning plans; completing them earns IBM-branded digital credentials (badges) that can be shared on LinkedIn or a CV. The university track includes project-based learning applying AI to real development tasks.

It is a credible, free way for students to explore tech careers and collect recognised badges before university.

about.en:
The College Board, which runs the SAT, provides free official preparation for the digital SAT. Its practice hub includes full-length practice tests taken in the Bluebook app (the same adaptive app used on test day, with scores and explanations), the Student Question Bank for targeted practice by skill and difficulty, a Study Plan Builder, Question of the Day, and guidance on how to use Khan Academy's free SAT practice.

Everything is free; you only need a College Board account. International students take the SAT at test centres worldwide, so practising in Bluebook is the best way to get used to the real interface.

For students applying to universities in the US and elsewhere that accept or require the SAT (see the university records on Meridian), official practice is the most reliable preparation available.

Free Student Question Bank and study plan builder
Official guidance on Khan Academy practice

eligibility.en: Anyone preparing for the SAT; free College Board account.

en: Create a free College Board account.
Download the Bluebook app and take a full-length practice test.
Review your score report and target weak skills in the Student Question Bank.
Use the Study Plan Builder and Khan Academy practice until test day.

costs.en: Free (the SAT exam itself is paid; fee waivers exist for eligible students).

score_reason: Essential free official SAT prep

IELTS is jointly owned by the British Council, IDP and Cambridge University Press & Assessment, and is accepted by thousands of universities worldwide. Its official preparation hub gathers free resources: official sample questions and answers for Listening, Reading, Writing and Speaking, videos explaining how the Writing test is scored, webinars, apps and links to teacher-led courses (some paid).

Using the official material helps you understand the exact format and band descriptors before you pay for the test, and to choose between IELTS Academic, General Training and IELTS for UKVI.

It is the right first step for any student who needs an English-language score for university applications or scholarships.

about.en:
UN SDG:Learn is a United Nations initiative that brings together learning offered by UN entities and partners on the Sustainable Development Goals. Learners can browse courses by SDG (from no poverty to partnerships for the goals) or by theme, and reach specialised community sites for statistics, evaluation, higher education and the Women2Lead initiative.

Courses are delivered on the providers' own platforms (for example UNITAR, UN CC:Learn, UNSSC and UN agencies); many are free and self-paced and award certificates of completion, while some professional courses are paid.

For students interested in MUN, international development or a UN career, it is the most direct way to find official UN training on any SDG.

about.en:
The Berkeley Math Tournament (BMT) is run by students at the University of California, Berkeley, and describes itself as the largest student-run maths competition in the world. Its flagship in-person tournament is on 14 November 2026; BMT 2026 Online is the synchronous online version for students who cannot travel to California.

BMT 2026 Online has an asynchronous Power Round (a proof-based team round) on 28–29 November 2026 and a live event on 5 December 2026 with the Guts round and Focus/General rounds, featuring original problems. Teams have up to 6 students (teams of 1 are allowed, but 4+ is recommended); students do not need to be from the same school and can form teams without a coach, with a Teammate Finder available. It is open to all students in grade 12 and below; students outside the US can email the organisers about grade equivalency.

Registration is on ContestDojo until 27 November 2026 (USD 8 per student; fee waivers for financial hardship), and a parent/guardian must sign UC Berkeley's consent waiver. It is an accessible way for students anywhere to try a top US university maths tournament.
